why: Gathering requirements and writing clear user stories is the core of a Business Analyst job. Case-study interviews ask you to do exactly this live.
outcome: run a discovery interview, write user stories with testable acceptance criteria, map gaps and prepare a UAT.

lessons.title: Discover the real need
text: People ask for solutions ('add an Excel export'); your job is to find the problem behind it ('the manager needs a weekly view of late orders'). Ask why, ask for examples, ask what happens today.
Identify stakeholders early: who uses it, who pays, who decides, who is impacted. Their goals often conflict.
points: Open questions: 'Walk me through the last time you did this'.
Capture current state (as-is) before designing the target (to-be).
Note business rules, exceptions and volumes: 'what if the client has two addresses?'.
Prioritise with MoSCoW: Must, Should, Could, Won't (this time).
Summarise and validate in writing after each workshop.

lessons.title: User stories and acceptance criteria
text: A user story describes a need from the user's point of view: As a <role>, I want <capability>, so that <benefit>. It is a placeholder for a conversation, not a full specification.
Acceptance criteria make the story testable. Given / When / Then (Gherkin) describes each scenario precisely.
points: INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.
Split big stories by workflow step, business rule or data variation, not by technical layer.
Cover the happy path, the errors and the edge cases in the criteria.
Attach mock-ups or examples when the UI matters.

example.code:
Story: As a job seeker, I want to filter offers by minimum salary,
       so that I only see offers I would accept.

Scenario: Offers below the minimum are hidden
  Given offers with salaries 35k, 45k and 60k
  When I set the minimum salary to 40k
  Then I see the 45k and 60k offers only

Scenario: Offers without a salary
  Given an offer with no salary information
  When I set a minimum salary
  Then the offer is shown with the label "Salary not specified"

lessons.title: Gap analysis and UAT
text: Gap analysis compares the current state with the target and lists what must change: process, data, tools, people. It turns a vision into a backlog.
User Acceptance Testing (UAT, 'recette' in French) is when business users confirm the solution meets their needs before go-live. The BA usually prepares and runs it.
points: Gap table columns: area, as-is, to-be, gap, action, owner, priority.
UAT test cases come from the acceptance criteria.
Each test case: preconditions, steps, expected result, actual result, status.
Log defects with steps to reproduce, severity and screenshots; agree go / no-go criteria up front.

lessons.title: Prioritise, trace and manage change
text: There is never time for everything. MoSCoW sorts requirements into Must, Should, Could and Won't (this time) with the stakeholders, so the release is defined by its Musts. Value versus effort and the cost of delay help break ties between Shoulds.

A traceability matrix links each requirement to its source, its user stories and its test cases: you can prove every Must is tested and see what a change affects. Changes will come; handle them with a light change process: describe it, assess the impact on scope, time and cost, decide with the sponsor, and update the backlog and the matrix.
points: If everything is a Must, nothing is: aim for about 60% of the effort on Musts.
Write down what is out of scope; it prevents most disputes.
Every change request gets an impact assessment before a yes.
Keep one source of truth (the backlog tool) rather than requirements scattered in emails.

example.code:
ID    Requirement                     Priority  Source          Story    Test case   Status
R-12  Export the claims list to CSV   Must      Claims manager  CL-88    TC-201/202  Done
R-13  Filter claims by status         Should    Workshop 03/10  CL-91    TC-210      In UAT
R-14  Email a weekly summary          Could     Director        -        -           Backlog
R-15  Mobile app                      Won't     -               -        -           Out of scope (v2)
example.note: One line per requirement: where it came from, how it is built and how it is tested.

items: Get from requested solution to real need
As a ..., I want ..., so that ...
Story is clear enough to start

pitfalls: Writing the solution the stakeholder asked for without understanding the problem.
Stories with no acceptance criteria, or criteria that cannot be tested ('the page is fast').
Forgetting edge cases and error cases.
Starting UAT without agreed exit criteria.

exercises.q: Rewrite as a user story: 'We need a CSV export button on the applications page'.
exercises.answer: As a job seeker, I want to download my applications as a file, so that I can share my progress with my career coach. (Then confirm with the user whether CSV, PDF or a share link best serves that goal.)

exercises.q: Write acceptance criteria for 'reset my password'.
exercises.answer:
Given I have an account
When I request a password reset with my email
Then I receive a reset link valid for 1 hour

Given the link has expired
When I open it
Then I see a message and can request a new link

Given I enter an unknown email
When I request a reset
Then I see the same confirmation message (no account disclosure)

exercises.q: Two stakeholders want contradictory features. What do you do?
exercises.answer: Make the conflict explicit with facts (goals, impact, cost), bring both to the decision-maker (often the Product Owner or sponsor) with options and a recommendation, and document the decision.

exercises.q: Two days before UAT, a director asks to add a new approval step to the process. What do you do?
exercises.answer: Thank them and capture the request precisely, then assess the impact with the team: process and screens to change, rules, tests, training, and the effect on the UAT date. Present the options to the sponsor: include it and move the date, deliver it in the next release, or swap it with a lower-priority item. Once decided, update the backlog, the traceability matrix and the test plan, and tell everyone affected.

interview.q: How do you gather requirements from a stakeholder who doesn't know what they want?
interview.a: Start from their current process and pain points, observe them working, use examples and quick mock-ups to react to, and iterate. People are better at reacting to something concrete than describing needs in the abstract.

interview.q: What makes a good user story?
interview.a: It follows INVEST: independent, negotiable, valuable to a user, estimable, small enough for a sprint, and testable thanks to clear acceptance criteria.

interview.q: What is your role in UAT?
interview.a: Prepare the test plan and cases from the acceptance criteria, organise the testers and environment, follow up defects with the team, report progress and help the business make the go / no-go decision.

interview.q: How do you handle conflicting priorities between two stakeholders?
interview.a: I make the conflict explicit with facts: what each request brings, its cost and its link to the project goal. I bring both stakeholders, or the sponsor who owns the decision, to agree on criteria such as value, risk and deadline, use MoSCoW or value versus effort to decide, and record the decision and its rationale in the backlog so it is not reopened every week.
